hook: Astronomers found Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, a pair of quasars, which are incredibly bright, active centers of distant galaxies.

sections.voiceover: Astronomers found Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, a pair of quasars, which are incredibly bright, active centers of distant galaxies.
sections.visual_cue: CGI animation of two bright, swirling quasars in deep space.
sections.sfx_cue: Low, rumbling space ambience with a sharp synth chime.
b_roll: CGI rendering of binary quasars from the early universe

text_overlay.text: Quasars at the Dawn of Time

sections.voiceover: Did the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy find this pair using Gemini North Telescope?
sections.visual_cue: Graphic showing the Gemini North Telescope pointing toward the distant, early universe.

sections.voiceover: The Gemini North Telescope shows these two massive black holes sit just 18,100 light-years apart.
sections.visual_cue: Split-screen comparison of the distance between the two quasars.

sections.voiceover: This distance is just one-fifth the diameter of our Milky Way galaxy. These massive objects existed 900 million years after the Big Bang.
sections.visual_cue: Side-by-side comparison of the Milky Way galaxy next to the 18,100 light-year gap.
b_roll: Milky Way galaxy spiral comparison graphic
Animation of two massive black holes orbiting each other

sections.voiceover: Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua contains two black holes weighing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the sun's mass.
sections.visual_cue: Slow zoom out into the vast, dark expanse of the early universe.
b_roll: Cinematic pan across the early universe
